subject: Computer Networking
title: UDP: Lightweight and Fast
description: A quick win: understand UDP: Lightweight and Fast.

hook.text: Sometimes you don't need every packet to arrive. You just need the ones that do to arrive fast.

buildup.text: UDP strips away handshakes and retransmissions. It sends datagrams and moves on immediately.

discovery.text: The header is tiny — just 8 bytes. Less overhead means less delay. Perfect for real-time applications.

twist.text: Lost a UDP packet? Gone forever. The protocol won't ask for it back. That's by design.

climax.text: Voice calls, video streams, and DNS lookups all choose UDP when speed beats perfection.

punchline.text: UDP is fire-and-forget. Fast, simple, no promises.

quiz.question: What makes UDP faster than TCP?

details.summary: UDP sends datagrams without establishing connections, tracking delivery, or guaranteeing order. This minimal overhead makes it ideal for time-sensitive applications like video streaming, online gaming, and DNS lookups where speed matters more than guaranteed delivery of every packet.
details.whyItMatters: UDP powers the real-time applications that users care about most. Understanding when to use UDP versus TCP is a fundamental network design decision.
takeaways: UDP sends datagrams with no connection setup or delivery guarantee
Lower overhead means less latency than TCP for each packet
Video streaming and gaming prefer UDP for real-time performance

faq.question: When should you use UDP instead of TCP?
faq.answer: Use UDP when speed matters more than reliability: live video, voice calls, online gaming, and DNS queries. A dropped video frame is better than a delayed one. TCP's retransmissions add latency that ruins real-time experiences. Many modern protocols build their own reliability on top of UDP.

faq.question: Is the UDP protocol unreliable?
faq.answer: UDP itself does not guarantee delivery, order, or duplicate protection. But applications can build reliability features on top of UDP as needed. QUIC, for example, runs over UDP and provides reliability comparable to TCP. UDP gives applications the freedom to choose their own trade-offs.
